sermon:
## The Two Ways: Psalm 1 and the Road That Ends Standing

*Why the Psalter refuses to give you a third option*

**Text:** Psalm 1 · **Supporting:** Deuteronomy 30:19; Jeremiah 17:7-8; Matthew 7:13-14; Galatians 6:7-8; Revelation 20:12

You were told there were more than two roads. The whole modern imagination is built on the promise of a third path, the reasonable middle, the private compromise, the life that keeps its options open and commits to nothing hard. Charles Taylor, the philosopher, described this in his 2007 book *A Secular Age* as the immanent frame: a world quietly closed at the top, where every road stays inside the room and no road leads anywhere final. In that frame there is no ultimate fork. There is only preference, and lifestyle, and the endless deferral of any choice that cannot be undone. The Psalter opens by shutting that door. Before it teaches you to pray, before it hands you a single lament or a single hymn of praise, it stands you at a fork and tells you there are two roads and only two, and one of them ends with you on your feet and one of them ends with you scattered like dust off a threshing floor.

Not three ways. Two.

### I. The Blessed Man Is a Planted Tree (Psalm 1:1-3)

The first word of the Hebrew Psalter is *ashrei*, blessed, happy, the deep flourishing of a life gone right at the root. It is not the shallow happiness of a mood. It is the settled well-being of a thing rightly ordered. And the psalm defines that flourishing first by what it walks away from. "Blessed is the man who walks not in the counsel of the wicked, nor stands in the way of sinners, nor sits in the seat of scoffers" (Psalm 1:1). Read the verbs slowly: walks, stands, sits. It is a descent, and the psalmist chose those verbs on purpose. You start by strolling near the counsel of the wicked, close enough to hear it, curious about it. Then you are standing in their road, no longer passing through but stopped, planted in the wrong soil. And one day you are sitting down in the scoffer's chair as if you had always lived there, comfortable, a permanent resident of contempt. Sin does not announce the descent. It never says: this is the first step down. It feels like curiosity, then like belonging, then like home.

- **A. The blessing is negative before it is positive**, Scripture defines the good life first by a refusal, three of them stacked, before it says one word about what the blessed man does. The man is blessed by what he will not join. We have inverted this completely. We define flourishing by what we accumulate and access and experience, by the doors we keep open, and we cannot understand why all the accumulation leaves us so thin. The psalm knew. A life is shaped as much by its refusals as by its embraces, and a man with no refusals has no shape at all.
- **B. Delight, not duty, does the rooting**, "his delight is in the law of the LORD, and on his law he meditates day and night" (Psalm 1:2). The Hebrew word for meditate, *hagah*, is not the quiet mind emptied of thought. It is the low growl of a lion over its prey, a muttering under the breath, the sound of a man chewing on something he cannot put down. This is not the scholar with a highlighter doing his required reading. This is a man who mutters the Word to himself on the drive and in the dark because he has tasted it and wants more of it. The rooting happens through delight, not discipline. Discipline without delight dries up and drifts.

And the result of that delight is a tree. "He is like a tree planted by streams of water that yields its fruit in its season, and its leaf does not wither. In all that he does, he prospers" (Psalm 1:3). Notice the word *planted*, the man did not root himself; he was set beside the stream by another hand. Jeremiah, the prophet, took this exact image six centuries later and pressed it harder: "Blessed is the man who trusts in the LORD, whose trust is the LORD. He is like a tree planted by water, that sends out its roots by the stream, and does not fear when heat comes, for its leaves remain green, and is not anxious in the year of drought, for it does not cease to bear fruit" (Jeremiah 17:7-8). Both the psalmist and the prophet knew the same thing about the tree, it does not fear the heat, because its roots are not in the weather. Rootedness is not something you feel. It is where you are planted, and the planting is grace before it is effort.

### II. The Wicked Are Chaff the Wind Drives Away (Psalm 1:4-6)

Then the hinge. The whole psalm turns on one word. "The wicked are not so, but are like chaff that the wind drives away" (Psalm 1:4). One word in the Hebrew, a flat, hard negation, *not so*, and the entire picture flips. The tree has weight, place, roots, a stream, a season, fruit. The chaff has none of it. Chaff is what is left on the threshing floor when the wheat is real and the husk is not, weightless, dry, the part of the harvest that gets thrown up into the moving air because it was never the point of the harvest to begin with. The wind does not have to work to take it. It simply lifts and it is gone.

- **A. The wicked are defined by weightlessness, not first by wickedness**, the psalm does not call them monsters. It does not describe their crimes. It calls them light. And that is the sharper indictment, the one we do not expect. A life with no roots and no delight and no place and no stream is not first evil; it is first empty. The judgment does not create the emptiness. It only reveals what was already there, that the whole life weighed nothing, and the wind of God's judgment finds nothing to hold it down.
- **B. Two roads, two destinies, no third**, "Therefore the wicked will not stand in the judgment, nor sinners in the congregation of the righteous; for the LORD knows the way of the righteous, but the way of the wicked will perish" (Psalm 1:5-6). Two ways, and the psalm ends by naming where each one arrives. Jesus took this exact shape up into the Sermon on the Mount and gave it a gate: "Enter by the narrow gate. For the gate is wide and the way is easy that leads to destruction, and those who enter by it are many. For the gate is narrow and the way is hard that leads to life, and those who find it are few" (Matthew 7:13-14). Paul closed the same fork in Galatians: "whatever one sows, that will he also reap. For the one who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption, but the one who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life" (Galatians 6:7-8). And Revelation ends the Bible standing at the same judgment, the dead judged "according to what they had done" (Revelation 20:12). The New Testament never softened Psalm 1. From the Sermon on the Mount to the last page, it sharpened it.

### III. Living Well When You Have Been Sold a Hundred Roads

Here is where I have to stop describing other people. I have preached the reasonable middle from my own pulpit. I have wanted a faith that keeps its options open, that walks near the counsel of the world for the sake of relevance, that stands a while in the way of sinners because I told myself I was building a bridge, that sits down in the scoffer's chair and calls it engagement with the culture. And I have called that maturity. I have called it wisdom. The psalm calls it the road that perishes. The descent from walking to standing to sitting is not a description of the pagan out there. It is a description of the pastor who thought he was strong enough to stroll near the edge.

The church has stood at this exact fork before, at national scale, and mostly chosen wrong. In May of 1934, in the city of Barmen in Germany, a small body of Christians looked at a national church that had baptized the reasonable middle, that had found a way to keep Christ and add the Führer, keep the cross and add the flag, keep the worship and add the ideology, and they wrote a declaration that said, in effect, there is no third way and there never was. "Jesus Christ, as he is attested for us in Holy Scripture, is the one Word of God whom we have to hear." Karl Barth drafted it. Most of the German church did not sign it. Most of the church chose the wide gate and called it patriotism, walked into the way of sinners and called it good citizenship, and history recorded which road perished. The Barmen Declaration is Psalm 1 written into the twentieth century. It insists the fork is real and binary when everyone around you swears it is a spectrum, when the whole air of the age tells you that only fools and fanatics believe there are just two ways.

- **A. The delight is the difference**, you will not walk the narrow road on willpower, and the psalm never asks you to. The tree is not straining and gritting its teeth to stay by the stream; it is being fed by it, drinking without effort. If your obedience is grim, joyless, teeth-clenched, then you have not yet found the delight the psalm is describing, and I can tell you from experience that grim obedience always drifts. It cannot hold. It walks, and then it stands, and then it sits down in the chair. Only delight keeps a man rooted, because only delight is stronger than the pull of the wide and easy road.
- **B. The blessed man in the end is one man**, read Psalm 1 honestly, with your own life in front of you, and you have already failed it. You have walked and stood and sat where you should not have. I have. Every reader of Psalm 1 is disqualified by Psalm 1. There is only one man who never walked in that counsel, never stood in that way, never sat in that seat, one true planted tree whose leaf never withered. And on a hill outside Jerusalem he was cut down like the wicked, treated as chaff, driven out of the city and blown into the dark of a Friday afternoon, so that the drifting rootless ones could be planted by the stream. He took the way that perishes so that our way would not. That is the only reason a chaff-man like me gets to stand in the judgment at all, not because I walked the road well, but because he walked mine.

Choose the road that ends standing.

## The King the Nations Rage Against: Psalm 2 and the Politics of Heaven

*Refuge or ruin, the offer hidden inside the rage*

**Text:** Psalm 2 · **Supporting:** Acts 4:25-27; Philippians 2:9-11; Hebrews 1:5; Revelation 19:15-16; John 3:36

Turn on anything. The rage is the water we swim in, nation against nation, party against party, the endless conviction that if we can only seize the levers of power we can force the world to bend the way we want it. Psalm 2 opens on exactly that noise. "Why do the nations rage and the peoples plot in vain?" (Psalm 2:1). Three thousand years old, and it reads like this morning's feed. But the psalm is not describing the news cycle. It is describing a conspiracy older than any nation and deeper than any election, the settled human refusal to be ruled by God at all. The rage on the surface is only the visible edge of a war that runs all the way down to the root of the human heart.

Not chaos. Coordination. The rage has a target, and the target is a throne.

### I. The Conspiracy of the Kings (Psalm 2:1-3)

"The kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers take counsel together, against the LORD and against his Anointed, saying, 'Let us burst their bonds apart and cast away their cords from us'" (Psalm 2:1-3). Notice what they want. Freedom. That is the whole cry, burst the bonds, throw off the cords, get out from under the rule. This is the oldest lie ever told, and it was first told in a garden: that God's rule is a chain and autonomy is the way up, that the cords are there to keep you small, and that the way to become like God is to cut them. The kings of Psalm 2 are the serpent's argument gone national, gone imperial, dressed up now in crowns and armies and platforms and slogans.

- **A. The rage is theological before it is political**, the peoples are not finally raging against a policy or a tax or a border. They are raging against being ruled at all, against the LORD and against his Anointed, his *Mashiach*, his Messiah. Strip any political fury down far enough and you find the same thing sitting at the bottom of it: a fury at the throne of heaven, a refusal of the one rule that would set everything else right. We think our rage is about the issue in front of us. The psalm says the issue is a mask over something far older.
- **B. The bonds they hate are the bonds that hold the world together**, this is the deep deception of the whole scene. They experience God's order as bondage, as cords cutting into the wrist. But the cords are precisely what keep the world from flying apart. Take away the rule of God and you do not get freedom; you get the war of every king against every other king, which is exactly the raging the psalm opens with. The human heart calls the tether a prison and calls the free fall liberty, and it has been making that mistake since Eden and paying for it ever since.

### II. The Laughter of Heaven and the Enthroned King (Psalm 2:4-9)

Then the scene cuts, upward, and the whole tone of the psalm changes. "He who sits in the heavens laughs; the Lord holds them in derision" (Psalm 2:4). This is not the cruel laughter of a tyrant enjoying the helplessness of his subjects. It is the laughter of absolute security. The nations imagine they are storming a fortress, massing at the walls, certain that this time they will finally pull the throne down. And the One inside is not even standing up. He is seated. He does not reach for a weapon. He laughs, not because their rage is amusing but because it is so completely beside the point. And then he speaks, and the speech is not a threat but an installation: "As for me, I have set my King on Zion, my holy hill" (Psalm 2:6). The raging was loud and long; the answer is quiet and total. The King is already installed. The conspiracy was over before it began, because the throne they came to take was never up for taking.

- **A. Heaven's response to human fury is not fury**, it is a coronation. God does not match the rage decibel for decibel, does not descend into the shouting match, does not stoop to argue with the kings on their terms. He seats his King, and that is the whole of his reply. The early church read this exactly so, and it steadied them in a moment of real fear. In Acts 4, hunted and threatened after the arrest of Peter and John, the believers prayed Psalm 2 back to God, "the kings of the earth set themselves, and the rulers were gathered together, against the Lord and against his Anointed", and they named Herod and Pontius Pilate and the Gentiles and the peoples of Israel as the raging kings of the psalm, gathered against Jesus, God's holy servant (Acts 4:25-27). Notice what they did not pray. They did not pray for the rage to stop. They prayed knowing the King was already on the hill, and that certainty is exactly why they could ask next for boldness instead of safety.
- **B. The Son is given the nations, not merely a nation**, "Ask of me, and I will make the nations your heritage, and the ends of the earth your possession" (Psalm 2:8). The scope is not one tribe or one land or one favored people. It is the ends of the earth. Hebrews takes verse 7, "You are my Son; today I have begotten you", and applies it straight to Christ, the Son the very angels must worship (Hebrews 1:5). Philippians finishes the thought and names the day it lands: God "highly exalted him and bestowed on him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, in heaven and on earth and under the earth, and every tongue confess that Jesus Christ is Lord" (Philippians 2:9-11). Every knee. The raging kings included. Revelation shows this same King riding out at the end of all things with a name written on his robe and on his thigh: "King of kings and Lord of lords" (Revelation 19:16). The plural is the whole point. Over all the kings of the earth, one King on Zion.

### III. Living Well While the Nations Rage

I have to name my own part in the raging, because it is far too easy to preach this psalm as though I stood safely outside the conspiracy, pointing at the kings. I do not stand outside it. I have wanted the church to seize the levers of power. I have looked at the culture and felt the old pull to burst somebody's bonds, to win by force what can only ever be won at a cross, to treat political power as the thing that will finally make the world safe for the gospel. That instinct feels like zeal from the inside. It is not zeal. It is the psalm's conspiracy quietly wearing a Christian coat. When the church rages for control, it has joined the kings and forgotten the King. It has decided, without saying so out loud, that the throne on Zion is not enough and it needs a throne in the capital too.

The church learned this the hard way, over the span of a thousand years. In 380 AD, with the Edict of Thessalonica, the emperor Theodosius made Nicene Christianity the official religion of the Roman Empire, and for a millennium after that the church confused the King on Zion with the kings of the earth. It reached for a sword it had been given no permission to hold. It burned dissenters and heretics. It baptized empire and called the whole arrangement Christendom. And every single time it grasped for the cords of power, it looked less like the One who was installed by heaven and more like the ones who raged against him, less like the laughing security of the enthroned God and more like the anxious kings massing at the walls, sure that everything depended on their grip. Lesslie Newbigin, the missionary bishop who spent decades in India and then came home to a post-Christian England, argued after his return in 1974 that the age of Christendom was over, and that this was mercy and not loss. The church, he said, was never meant to rule the West by force from the hill; it was meant to bear witness to the King who already rules it. Our job is not to storm Zion or to install ourselves on any earthly throne. Our job is far smaller and far harder than that. Kiss the Son.

- **A. The psalm ends not with a threat but an offer**, "Serve the LORD with fear, and rejoice with trembling. Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and you perish in the way, for his wrath is quickly kindled. Blessed are all who take refuge in him" (Psalm 2:11-12). The raging nations, having done their worst against the throne, are handed a door. Refuge instead of ruin. The King they conspired against opens his arms to the conspirators and pronounces them blessed if they will only come. The psalm that began with a war between the nations and the throne ends with an invitation, and the invitation is aimed straight at the very kings who started the war.
- **B. The King who was raged against became the one raged upon**, Acts 4 is the hinge of the whole psalm. The nations that gathered against the Anointed did their absolute worst, and their worst turned out to be a cross. The installed King let himself be uninstalled, mocked with a crown of thorns pressed down as a cruel joke, executed by the kings of the earth acting exactly as Psalm 2 said they always would. And heaven's laughter, the unshakable laughter of the God who could not be moved, turned out on the third morning to be an empty tomb. The refuge the psalm offers is not cheap and it is not sentimental. "Whoever believes in the Son has eternal life; whoever does not obey the Son shall not see life, but the wrath of God remains on him" (John 3:36). The door is wide open, but it was opened at the cost of the King's own blood. That is exactly why it is real, and why the raging can finally end at his feet instead of on a battlefield.

Rage ends at the King's feet.

## How Long, O Lord: Psalm 13 and the Prayer of the Waiting

*Lament is permitted prayer, and it has a shape*

**Text:** Psalm 13 · **Supporting:** Habakkuk 1:2; Revelation 6:10; Lamentations 3:22-23; Romans 8:24-25; 2 Corinthians 4:8-9

You were taught, somewhere along the way, that a strong faith does not complain. That the mature Christian smiles through it, keeps the tone positive, trusts quietly, and never lets God hear the raw thing. So when the raw thing comes, the diagnosis that will not reverse, the silence that stretches into years, the prayer you have prayed a thousand times into what feels like a shut and locked sky, you assume your ache is a failure of faith. You decide that the honest cry rising in you is the thing to be ashamed of, the thing to swallow. Psalm 13 was put in the Bible to tell you it is not. It is not weakness dressed up as prayer. It is prayer. God preserved a man's complaint as Scripture, canonized his ache, gave it chapter and verse, so that yours would have somewhere to go.

Four times: how long.

### I. The Fourfold Complaint (Psalm 13:1-2)

"How long, O LORD? Will you forget me forever? How long will you hide your face from me? How long must I take counsel in my soul and have sorrow in my heart all the day? How long shall my enemy be exalted over me?" (Psalm 13:1-2). Four hammer-blows of the same Hebrew phrase, *ad-anah*, how long, how long, how long, how long. And notice who he blames. Not the enemy first. Not the circumstances. God first. "Will you forget me... will you hide your face." He is not filing a complaint about his hardship to a sympathetic bystander who might carry the message along to God. He is charging God, to God's own face, with forgetting him and with hiding. The complaint does not go sideways. It goes straight up.

- **A. Biblical lament aims its complaint upward**, the psalmist does not vent to a friend and then stay carefully polite when he finally turns to God. He brings the accusation directly to the throne, out loud, and Scripture prints it and calls it prayer. Habakkuk the prophet did the very same thing: "O LORD, how long shall I cry for help, and you will not hear? Or cry to you 'Violence!' and you will not save?" (Habakkuk 1:2). The martyrs under the altar in Revelation do it too, in heaven itself, after they have already died for their faith and are supposedly beyond all complaint: "How long, O Lord, holy and true, until you judge and avenge our blood?" (Revelation 6:10). If the saints in glory can still cry *how long*, then the cry is not immaturity to grow out of. Heaven can take the question. It is our theology, not God's throne, that turns out to be too fragile for it.
- **B. The ache has a clock in it**, *how long* is a very particular prayer, and its particularity matters. It is not the cry of a man who has decided God will never act. It is the cry of a man who believes God will act and cannot bear the length of the interval before he does. It is faith stretched thin over time, faith that has not yet been answered and refuses to go quiet about it. Despair does not say *how long*, because despair has stopped expecting any answer at all and therefore stopped bothering to ask. Lament is the opposite of despair. It is the prayer of a person who is still waiting precisely because he still believes there is Someone worth waiting on.

### II. The Turn to Petition (Psalm 13:3-4)

Then the complaint becomes a request, and this turn is the hinge of the whole psalm. "Consider and answer me, O LORD my God; light up my eyes, lest I sleep the sleep of death, lest my enemy say, 'I have prevailed over him,' lest my foes rejoice because I am shaken" (Psalm 13:3-4). The grief has not lifted. Read it against verses 1 and 2, nothing in his situation has changed. But the prayer itself has moved. It stopped circling the wound and started asking for something specific: light up my eyes, keep me back from the sleep of death. This is the structure Scripture keeps handing us, the shape of nearly every biblical lament. Complaint is permitted, fully and freely permitted, but complaint is not the destination. Lament walks. It moves from the raw cry toward the specific asking, and a lament that never once turns to petition has quietly curdled into something else.

- **A. Petition is what keeps lament from becoming bitterness**, the difference between a prayer and a grudge is a small and enormous thing: a prayer still asks. The man who has stopped asking has quietly concluded that God will not answer, and a conclusion like that hardens over the years into a settled resentment that no longer bothers to bring anything to God at all. The psalmist keeps his hand out. Even in the dark, even with the enemy still exalted over him and rejoicing, he is still reaching toward God for something specific. That reaching is faith, however thin it has worn, and it is the thing that keeps the dark from becoming permanent.
- **B. He prays his weakness, not his strength**, "lest I sleep the sleep of death." He does not tell God that he can hold on a little longer, does not perform his own resilience for heaven's benefit. He tells God plainly that he cannot make it without an answer, that he is near the sleep of death and only God can light up his eyes and keep him from it. Paul knew this exact ground and named it precisely: "We are afflicted in every way, but not crushed; perplexed, but not driven to despair; persecuted, but not forsaken; struck down, but not destroyed" (2 Corinthians 4:8-9). The not-crushed and the not-destroyed are always God's doing, never the sufferer's grip. The psalmist prays as a man who already knows this, that whatever finally keeps him from the sleep of death will have to come from outside himself, from the God he is crying to.

### III. Living Well in the Long Silence

I have sat in my own office with people who prayed for years into what felt like a shut sky, and I have not always had the courage to let them lament. I have rushed the hurting toward the happy ending because their pain made me uncomfortable, and in that moment my own discomfort mattered more to me than their honesty. I handed them a verse to fix the ache instead of a shoulder to help carry it. That is a pastoral sin, and I have committed it more than once, and I know it. And the church at large has too often functioned as the enemy of lament, hurrying the grieving through the four *how longs* to get to the praise as quickly as possible, treating the complaint as a stain to be scrubbed out rather than a prayer to be prayed. We have quietly made our own people ashamed of the exact words God took the trouble to preserve for them.

There is an old wisdom here that the modern church quietly threw away. For most of Christian history the church prayed the Psalms straight through, all of them, in order, on a repeating cycle. The sixth-century Rule of Benedict required monks to pray the entire Psalter every single week, which meant they could not curate their spiritual life down to the songs that happened to feel encouraging. They prayed the laments exactly as often as they prayed the hymns of joy. They could not skip Psalm 13. They could not build a faith of only the sunny psalms, because the discipline itself handed them the dark ones on schedule whether they felt like praying them or not. When we reduced our worship down to the psalms that make us feel good, we lost the vocabulary for the night. And then we wondered why our people fall apart in the dark with nothing to say to God, no words at all for the hour when the sky goes silent, because we had thrown away the very words the church had spent fifteen centuries keeping in her mouth precisely for that hour.

- **A. Trust is a decision made before the circumstances change**, the psalm ends in a way that should stop us: "But I have trusted in your steadfast love; my heart shall rejoice in your salvation. I will sing to the LORD, because he has dealt bountifully with me" (Psalm 13:5-6). Read that against verses 1 and 2 one more time. Nothing external has moved. The enemy is still exalted. The answer has not come. The face of God is not yet visibly turned back toward him. And he sings anyway. The Hebrew word is *chesed*, steadfast, covenant, loyal love, and it is what he leans his entire weight on while the evidence for it is still absent. He does not wait until he feels bountifully dealt with before he says it. He says it, in the dark, as a deliberate act of trust. Lamentations, written by a man sitting in the smoking ashes of a burned Jerusalem, says the same thing over the rubble: "The steadfast love of the LORD never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness" (Lamentations 3:22-23). That was not written over a happy ending. It was written over ruins.
- **B. The One who cried how long got no answer for three hours**, on the cross Jesus prayed the deepest lament in the whole Psalter, "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me," and heaven stayed silent while he died, hour after hour, the sky itself gone dark over the city. He walked the full length of the unanswered prayer, all the way to the very bottom of it, so that ours would never again be prayed into a truly empty sky. Paul reminds us that "in this hope we were saved. Now hope that is seen is not hope. For who hopes for what he sees? But if we hope for what we do not see, we wait for it with patience" (Romans 8:24-25). We wait, but we do not wait alone, and we do not wait into a void. When you cry *how long* now, you are crying it to a God who has been exactly where you are, whose own silence on a Friday broke open into a Sunday morning. The answer was late, by every human clock in Jerusalem. But it came.

Sing trust before the answer comes.

## Forsaken, Then Heard: Psalm 22 and the Cry Jesus Made His Own

*The lament that becomes a congregation stretching to the ends of the earth*

**Text:** Psalm 22 · **Supporting:** Matthew 27:46; Mark 15:34; John 19:24; Hebrews 2:12; Isaiah 53:3

There is a kind of pain that does not want company and does not want advice. It does not want your verse or your reasoning or your gentle reminder that everything happens for a reason. It wants to know one thing only, whether God is still there at all. Psalm 22 is the prayer for that hour, and it begins where most of us are far too afraid to begin: with the raw, naked possibility that he is not. "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me? Why are you so far from saving me, from the words of my groaning? O my God, I cry by day, but you do not answer, and by night, but I find no rest" (Psalm 22:1-2). This is the deepest lament in the whole Psalter, and the Bible does not flinch from putting the word *forsaken* in a believer's mouth and then calling the entire thing prayer.

Forsaken. Then, before it ends, heard.

### I. The Cry Out of God-Forsakenness (Psalm 22:1-2, 6-8)

The psalm holds two unbearable things at once, and it refuses to let go of either one to make itself easier. God is absent, "far from saving me," silent by day and silent by night, and yet he is still "my God." Twice in the very first verse: my God, my God. The forsaken man does not let go of the God who seems to have let go of him. He clings, hard, to the very One he is accusing of absence. And then the mockery comes pouring in on top of the silence. "But I am a worm and not a man, scorned by mankind and despised by the people. All who see me mock me; they make mouths at me; they wag their heads; 'He trusts in the LORD; let him deliver him; let him rescue him, for he delights in him'" (Psalm 22:6-8). The suffering is doubled, and it is precise. The silence of heaven above him, and the scorn of men all around him. Isaiah's suffering servant stands in the very same place seven centuries later, "despised and rejected by men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with grief; and as one from whom men hide their faces he was despised, and we esteemed him not" (Isaiah 53:3).

- **A. Faith and forsakenness are not opposites here**, the psalmist clings and accuses in a single breath, and Scripture prints the whole thing as a model prayer. We tend to treat the feeling of abandonment as proof that our faith has collapsed, as evidence to be hidden from other people and from God. Scripture treats it as something a believer prays, out loud, to the God he cannot feel. The mere presence of the word *forsaken* in a psalm does not mean the faith behind it has failed. It means the faith is still talking, still praying, still addressing the God it cannot sense.
- **B. The mockery uses his own theology against him**, "he trusts in the LORD; let him deliver him." This is the cruelest wound in the entire psalm, sharper than the physical pain. It is not merely that they hate him; it is that they take his own faith and turn it into the punchline. They taunt him that his trust was a fool's bet all along, that the God he leaned his whole life on has plainly and visibly abandoned him now, that his entire religion was self-deception finally exposed for everyone to see. Every sufferer who has ever heard the words "where is your God now" has stood exactly here, in verse 8, with the enemy weaponizing his own faith against him.

### II. The Turn to Remembered Faithfulness (Psalm 22:3-5, 9-11)

But the cry does not stay in the pit, and this is the anatomy of biblical lament, it moves, it climbs. Between the complaints, the psalmist keeps reaching backward, hauling himself up hand over hand by memory. "Yet you are holy, enthroned on the praises of Israel. In you our fathers trusted; they trusted, and you delivered them. To you they cried and were rescued; in you they trusted and were not put to shame" (Psalm 22:3-5). And then it gets even more intimate, even more personal, the memory reaching all the way back to before he could remember: "Yet you are he who took me from the womb; you made me trust you at my mother's breasts. On you was I cast from my birth, and from my mother's womb you have been my God" (Psalm 22:9-10). He fights the present silence with remembered faithfulness. He cannot feel God now, so he rehearses instead what God has already done, for the fathers who cried and were rescued and were not put to shame, and for him personally, from the womb, before he could even speak a word.

- **A. Memory is a weapon against the present dark**, when the felt presence of God is gone, the recorded faithfulness of God is what the sufferer holds onto with both hands. The psalmist does not manufacture a warm feeling to paper over the pain. He does something harder and truer than that: he recalls a history. He preaches to himself the long track record of a God who delivered the fathers and carried him from the womb, and he lets that history argue back against the present silence. This is exactly what faith does in the dark, it does not pretend the dark away, and it does not lie to itself about how black the dark has become; it remembers the light it can no longer see, and it lets the remembered light stand as evidence against the present silence. There is a kind of stubbornness in this that we have mistaken for weakness. The man who keeps rehearsing what God has done, even while feeling nothing, is not in denial. He is doing the hardest work faith ever does: holding the record steady when the feeling has fled the room entirely.
- **B. The lament is honest about both, the silence and the record**, the psalm does not resolve its own tension by denying the pain, and it does not resolve it by denying the past. It holds both in the same two hands at once. God is silent now; God has been faithful before. Both are completely true, and the psalmist refuses to collapse either one just to make himself more comfortable. He keeps on praying inside the tension instead of escaping out of it, and that costly honesty is exactly what the modern church has nearly lost the ability to bear.

### III. Living Well Under a Silent Sky, and the Cross That Fills It

I want to be careful not to stand outside this psalm as a commentator handing down tidy observations, because I have preached a triumphant, resolved, tidy God to people whose sky was silent, and I have offered them my own certainty when what they actually needed was permission to say *forsaken* out loud and still be counted among the believers. The church often cannot tolerate the middle of Psalm 22 at all. It wants to rush straight to the ending. It hurries the dying past verses 1 through 21 to get to the resurrection, and it leaves people alone in the dark of Saturday with no words in their mouths. But the psalm itself will not permit that. It makes you live through the whole long descent before it grants you a single note of hope. It will not let you skip the cry to reach the comfort.

And then there is the one fact that changes absolutely everything about this psalm. On a Friday afternoon on a hill outside Jerusalem, a man hanging on a Roman cross cried its opening line aloud in Aramaic, "Eli, Eli, lema sabachthani? which means, My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?" (Matthew 27:46; Mark 15:34). Jesus did not quote Psalm 22 as a fitting and poetic illustration of his mood. He prayed it as his own prayer, from the inside. He entered the God-forsakenness the psalm describes and he drank it all the way down to the bottom of the cup, not merely the feeling of abandonment but the actual severing, the real thing, so that the ones who genuinely deserve to be forsaken never finally are. And the details around the cross fell into place with a precision that should stop your breath. The soldiers gambling for his clothing at the foot of the cross fulfilled verse 18 to the very letter, "they divide my garments among them, and for my clothing they cast lots" (Psalm 22:18; John 19:24), as if the whole scene had been written down and set aside a thousand years before it happened. Because it had.

- **A. The psalm does not end forsaken, it ends worldwide**, read all the way to the bottom of it and the pit gives way to a gathering that fills the earth. "All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the LORD, and all the families of the nations shall worship before you. For kingship belongs to the LORD, and he rules over the nations" (Psalm 22:27-28). The cry of one abandoned man in the first verse becomes, by the last, a congregation that stretches to the ends of the earth. Hebrews takes verse 22 and puts it directly into the mouth of the risen Christ: "I will tell of your name to my brothers; in the midst of the congregation I will sing your praise" (Hebrews 2:12). The forsaken one, on the far side of his forsaking, stands up in the middle of a congregation and gathers the very family he died to make. The psalm that opened utterly alone ends in a room crowded with every nation on earth.
- **B. Your dark Saturday sits inside his answered Friday**, because Jesus prayed the whole psalm, both the forsaking and the vindication, you never pray verse 1 alone again. When your own sky goes silent, you are crying into the same dark that he entered, and his dark came out at verse 27, at the ends of the earth, at the empty tomb. The forsaken cry of Golgotha was heard. Heaven's silence over that hill lasted three hours, and then it broke. That is precisely why yours will break too, not because your pain is small or your dark is short, but because the deepest forsaking in the history of the world has already been answered, and yours is now folded up inside his.

The forsaken cry was finally answered.

## The Shepherd in the Valley: Psalm 23 and the Presence That Is Enough

*Not the absence of trouble, the presence of God in it*

**Text:** Psalm 23 · **Supporting:** John 10:11; Ezekiel 34:11-12; Hebrews 13:5; Romans 8:38-39; 1 Peter 2:25

Psalm 23 has been read at so many funerals and printed on so many cards that we have nearly killed it with familiarity. We hear it now as comfort food, a soft blanket of a psalm, gentle background music for grief. But read it slowly, as if you had never heard it before, and it is not soft at all. It is a psalm about walking through a valley of deep darkness, through the very shadow of death itself, and its whole claim is not that the darkness disappears but that Someone is down in it with you. The comfort of Psalm 23 is not the absence of the valley. It is the presence of the Shepherd inside the valley. Strip that presence out and the psalm has nothing whatsoever to say to anyone who is actually in the dark.

Not safety from the dark. Company in it.

### I. The Shepherd Who Provides and Restores (Psalm 23:1-3)

"The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want. He makes me lie down in green pastures. He leads me beside still waters. He restores my soul. He leads me in paths of righteousness for his name's sake" (Psalm 23:1-3). Start with the scandal buried inside the metaphor. Sheep are not admirable animals. They are not noble or clever or self-sufficient in any way. They are helpless, prone to wander off a cliff without noticing, unable to find water on their own or defend themselves against anything with teeth. To call yourself a sheep is to confess, flatly and without flattery, that you cannot run your own life, that left entirely alone you will get lost or get eaten. And the very first thing this Shepherd does for such a creature is *make* it lie down, the Hebrew verb is causative, an action done to the sheep from outside, because a sheep too anxious to rest will not rest on its own initiative. It has to be settled by the near presence of the shepherd before it can stop scanning the horizon for the next threat.

- **A. "I shall not want" is a claim about the Shepherd, not about the sheep's circumstances**, it does not mean the sheep gets everything it craves. It means the sheep lacks nothing it truly needs, because the One leading it is enough. Contentment, then, is not the absence of all desire, and it is not the arrival of everything wanted. It is the presence of a Shepherd you actually trust to lead you to what you genuinely need. The whole first line is a confession that the sheep's entire security rests not in itself but in the competence and the character of the One holding the staff.
- **B. Restoration is the Shepherd's work, not the sheep's discipline**, "he restores my soul." The Hebrew word here is *nephesh*, and it is not one part of a person; it is the whole life, the self, the very center that animates the body. And the sheep does not restore its own soul by trying harder or resolving to do better next time. It is restored by being led, to the water it could never have found by itself, to the pasture it could not have reached, back onto the path it had already wandered off of. This is exactly the God that Ezekiel promised, the shepherd who does the finding and the rescuing himself: "For thus says the Lord GOD: Behold, I, I myself will search for my sheep and will seek them out... I will rescue them from all places where they have been scattered on a day of clouds and thick darkness" (Ezekiel 34:11-12). I, I myself. The Shepherd does the work the sheep cannot.

### II. The Shepherd Who Walks Through the Valley (Psalm 23:4-5)

Then the psalm turns, and something remarkable and easily missed happens to the pronouns as it turns. Up through verse 4 the Shepherd is "he", spoken about, described from a certain reverent distance. But in the valley he suddenly becomes "you", spoken to directly, face to face, intimately. "Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for you are with me; your rod and your staff, they comfort me" (Psalm 23:4). Read that shift again and let it register. The valley of deep shadow is exactly the place where the psalmist stops talking about God at a distance and starts talking to him up close. Intimacy with the Shepherd does not deepen in the green pasture, where everything is easy and safe. It deepens in the dark, where everything is not.

- **A. The promise is company, not exemption**, "I walk through." Not around the valley. Not over it or above it or safely to one side of it. Through the middle of it. The Shepherd does not airlift the sheep out of the valley of the shadow of death the moment it gets frightening and dark. He walks the length of it with them, step for step, the rod in his hand to beat back the predators that wait in the dark and the staff in his hand to hook the sheep back when it drifts toward the edge. The comfort the psalmist names is not rescue from the valley. It is the with-ness of the Shepherd inside the valley. "For you are with me", that one small phrase, sitting right at the exact center of the psalm, is the whole thing the psalm exists to say.
- **B. The table is set in the presence of enemies**, "You prepare a table before me in the presence of my enemies; you anoint my head with oil; my cup overflows" (Psalm 23:5). Notice carefully what the psalm does not say. It does not say the enemies are destroyed first, or driven off, or made to vanish so that the meal can be enjoyed in peace and quiet. The feast is spread while the enemies are still watching, in full view of the threat, the cup running over while the foes look on and can do nothing to stop it. God's provision is not the removal of every danger before the blessing arrives. It is abundance set out in the very middle of the danger, a table laid in the shadow of the ones who wish you harm.

### III. Living Well in a Culture That Cannot Sit Still

I have to confess that I do not always want a Shepherd. If I am honest with myself, I want a map and a head start and the private dignity of finding the water on my own. The whole instinct of my age, and it is mine as much as it belongs to anyone else, is the refusal to be led, the deep and flattering conviction that dependence is weakness and that the mature adult manages his own valley without needing to be carried through it by anybody. James K. A. Smith, the philosopher, argued in his 2009 book *Desiring the Kingdom* that we are formed far less by what we consciously believe than by what we love, and that what we love is trained, quietly and relentlessly, day after day, by our habits and our small daily liturgies. We have spent a whole generation training ourselves through those habits to love autonomy and self-management above nearly everything else, and then we walk into the valley of the shadow of death with a soul so thoroughly shaped to refuse help that we can no longer receive the one thing that would actually carry us through it, a Shepherd we are willing to simply follow.

The oldest confession of the church knew this better than we do. The catacombs dug beneath the city of Rome in the second and third centuries are covered in one image, scratched again and again into the stone above the graves of the Christian dead, not yet the cross, which was not there, but a young man with a lamb slung across his shoulders. The Good Shepherd. Christians dying under Roman persecution buried their loved ones underneath the picture of the Shepherd who walks the valley, because they had staked everything they had, including their own bodies, on Psalm 23 being true on the far side of the grave. They did not carve an image of safety onto those tombs. They did not carve an image of a comfortable life without a valley in it. They carved an image of company in the valley, a Shepherd carrying a helpless sheep, and they laid their dead down beneath it in hope.

- **A. The valley of the shadow includes the last one**, Psalm 23 is read at funerals for a reason, and the reason is not that it is sentimental. The Shepherd walks the valley of the shadow of death, the actual valley, the final one, the one none of us gets around, and he comes out the far side of it, and the sheep comes out with him: "and I shall dwell in the house of the LORD forever" (Psalm 23:6). This is not merely a psalm about getting through a hard week or a rough patch. It is a psalm about getting through death itself in the company of a Shepherd who has already walked that particular valley before us and knows exactly the way out. Paul says the very same thing in different words: neither death nor life "will be able to separate us from the love of God in Christ Jesus our Lord" (Romans 8:38-39).
- **B. The Shepherd became the Lamb**, Jesus stood up one day and said it plainly to a crowd: "I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep" (John 10:11). The One with the rod and the staff walked down into the darkest valley of them all himself, and he did not come back up out of it until he had killed the thing that was waiting there in the dark for us. He became a lamb, the Lamb, and let himself be led like a lamb to slaughter, so that the sheep could follow him safely through. Peter names the whole turn in one clean line: "For you were straying like sheep, but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of your souls" (1 Peter 2:25). And over the whole of it stands the promise the Shepherd made and will never break: "I will never leave you nor forsake you" (Hebrews 13:5).

Goodness follows you all the way.

## Create in Me a Clean Heart: Psalm 51 and the Prayer That Refuses to Bargain

*David's confession, and why it asks for re-creation instead of relief*

**Text:** Psalm 51 · **Supporting:** 2 Samuel 12:13; Romans 3:23; 1 John 1:9; Ezekiel 36:26; 2 Corinthians 5:17

We are experts at the managed apology. We say we are sorry in a way that quietly protects us. We confess the tidy version of the sin that keeps our dignity intact, the sanitized summary that admits just enough to seem humble and hides just enough to stay safe. We blame the circumstances that pushed us there, the pressure, the exhaustion, the other person, the bad week. And we promise to do better, and we mean the promise as a bargain, a trade offered up to God so that he will lift the guilt and let us move along. Psalm 51 is a man walking away from every single piece of that. It is David after the prophet Nathan has cornered him over Bathsheba and over the arranged murder of her husband Uriah, and it is the least self-protective prayer in the entire Bible. He does not manage this. He does not spin it or frame it or soften it. He lays the whole thing bare on the ground before God and asks for the one thing no guilty man can ever manufacture for himself, a new heart.

Not relief. Re-creation.

### I. The Confession That Hides Nothing (Psalm 51:1-4)

"Have mercy on me, O God, according to your steadfast love; according to your abundant mercy blot out my transgressions. Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin. For I know my transgressions, and my sin is ever before me. Against you, you only, have I sinned and done what is evil in your sight" (Psalm 51:1-4). Read carefully what David does not do here. He does not minimize, "my sin is ever before me," it will not leave him alone, it stands in front of his eyes every waking hour of every day. He does not deflect the blame onto Bathsheba, or onto the war, or onto the loneliness and pressure of wearing the crown. And most startling of all, "against you, you only, have I sinned." He had wronged Uriah, a loyal soldier he had arranged to have killed to cover his tracks. He had wronged Bathsheba, and the child, and the whole nation that trusted him. And yet David knows that every sin, whatever human wreckage it leaves scattered behind it, is finally and most deeply a sin against God, because God is the one whose law was broken and whose face was despised in the doing of it.

- **A. Real confession names the sin as sin, not a mistake**, David reaches for three separate words in these opening verses: transgression, iniquity, sin. Rebellion, crookedness, missing the mark entirely. He does not reach for the softer vocabulary we so badly prefer, the words that quietly turn a sin into a slip, a failure, a lapse in judgment, an error. He calls it exactly what it is. And Paul flattens all of our careful little distinctions anyway: "for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God" (Romans 3:23). There is no grade of sin small enough to slip beneath that verdict, and David does not waste any effort trying to find one.
- **B. Confession that bargains is not confession**, David asks for mercy "according to your steadfast love," according to God's *chesed*, God's covenant loyalty, and not according to any deal that David himself can put on the table. He brings nothing whatsoever to trade, no promise, no penance, no offer of future good behavior to sweeten the request. He simply throws his whole weight onto mercy. And this is exactly why the mercy came to him. When Nathan first confronted him with the parable and the accusation, David said only five words: "I have sinned against the LORD." And Nathan answered him at once, "The LORD also has put away your sin; you shall not die" (2 Samuel 12:13). The forgiveness arrived in the very moment the bargaining stopped and the real confession began.

### II. The Plea for a Clean Heart (Psalm 51:5-12)

Then David asks God for something impossible. Not "help me try harder next time." Not "give me one more chance to prove myself and make it up to you." He asks something no one has any business asking: "Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me" (Psalm 51:10). The Hebrew verb is *bara*, the exact same word used in Genesis 1 for what God did when he made the entire world out of nothing at all. It is a word the Old Testament reserves almost entirely for God alone, because only God does that particular kind of making. David does not ask to be improved, or repaired, or gently upgraded. He asks to be made new from scratch, created fresh out of nothing, because he has finally understood that his real problem was never his behavior but his heart, and a man can no more re-create his own heart than the dust of the ground could have organized itself into a living, breathing creature back in the beginning.

- **A. The problem goes all the way down to the root**, "Behold, I was brought forth in iniquity, and in sin did my mother conceive me" (Psalm 51:5). David is not blaming his mother here, and he is not complaining about the circumstances of his birth. He is confessing something far more serious: that his catastrophe with Bathsheba was not a one-time slip from an otherwise clean and healthy man. It came up out of a heart that was bent from the very start, a nature that was crooked before he ever chose anything at all. This is precisely why he cannot fix it with better resolutions or firmer discipline. You cannot manage a heart problem with improved behavior any more than you can cure a diseased tree by carefully tying better fruit onto its branches. The trouble is in the root, and only the root will do.
- **B. He asks for creation, and only God creates**, "Renew a right spirit within me... Restore to me the joy of your salvation, and uphold me with a willing spirit" (Psalm 51:10-12). David is asking God to perform a creative act inside him that David has no power to perform on himself. And Ezekiel, generations later, promised exactly this act of God as the beating heart of the new covenant: "And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you. And I will remove the heart of stone from your flesh and give you a heart of flesh" (Ezekiel 36:26). David is asking, centuries early and almost word for word, for the exact miracle that God would one day promise to pour out on his people, the surgery on the heart that no sinner has ever been able to perform on himself.

### III. Living Well When You Have Done the Thing You Swore You Never Would

I have prayed the managed apology to God more times than I can count, and I have prayed it from a pulpit, which is worse, because a pulpit takes private evasion and turns it into public performance. I have confessed the sin that costs me nothing to admit while carefully burying the one sin that would actually cost me something real to name. I have wanted relief from the guilt without the exposure of the confession, I have wanted the clean feeling without the naked honesty that alone produces it, and then I have called that repentance. It was not repentance. It was negotiation with God, a quiet attempt to get the pardon while keeping the dignity. Psalm 51 will not let me negotiate. It stands in front of every managed apology I have ever offered from any pulpit and asks me whether I am willing to be exposed the way David let himself be exposed.

The church has wrestled with this psalm's raw honesty for centuries, and one man's story shows exactly why it matters so much. In the year 386, in a garden in Milan, a brilliant and thoroughly self-managed man named Augustine, a man who had spent years arranging his sins into respectable categories, always intending to repent tomorrow, always fully confident that he could reform himself on his own chosen timetable, heard a child's voice nearby chanting "take up and read," opened Paul's letter to the Romans at random, read a few lines, and broke. He would later write in his *Confessions* that the human will simply cannot heal itself, that grace has to go all the way down to the very root of a man, that a person cannot possibly lift himself out of the pit using the very same will that is already down in the pit alongside him. That is Psalm 51 happening again in a garden, three centuries after David knelt. Augustine did not finally ask God to help him become a slightly better version of himself. He asked, exactly like David before him, to be remade from the ground up, because he had at last seen the same thing David saw: that a bent will cannot straighten itself, and a dead heart cannot resurrect itself, and the only real hope for either is a God who creates out of nothing.

- **A. The broken heart is the acceptable offering**, "For you will not delight in sacrifice, or I would give it; you will not be pleased with a burnt offering. The sacrifices of God are a broken spirit; a broken and contrite heart, O God, you will not despise" (Psalm 51:16-17). David had discovered something startling: that God did not want the covering sacrifice of a bull to smooth this whole matter over and let both parties quietly move on. God wanted the man himself, broken, honest, holding nothing back, hiding no corner of it. That kind of shattered, exposed honesty is the only altar God actually accepts, and it is exactly the one altar our managed apologies never once get around to building. And John says it plainly to us on this side of the cross: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness" (1 John 1:9).
- **B. The clean heart was bought at a bloodier altar than David knew**, David asked to be re-created, and the re-creation cost far more than he could possibly see from where he knelt. "Therefore, if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old has passed away; behold, the new has come" (2 Corinthians 5:17). The clean heart that David begged God to make is now handed freely to us, and it is handed to us precisely because Christ took the unclean one, took mine, all the way to a cross and let it be destroyed there in his own body. He was made sin, Scripture says, so that a lifelong self-manager like me could finally stop managing, stop negotiating, stop offering God the sanitized summary, and simply kneel all the way down and be remade from nothing.

Broken before God is mended.

## A Refuge When the Earth Gives Way: Psalm 46 and the Command to Be Still

*Not a call to calm, a summons to stop striving*

**Text:** Psalm 46 · **Supporting:** Exodus 14:14; Isaiah 26:3; Matthew 8:26; Philippians 4:6-7; Zephaniah 3:17

"Be still, and know that I am God" is embroidered on more pillows and printed on more coffee mugs than any other verse in the Old Testament, and almost every one of them gets the line badly wrong. We hear it as a gentle invitation to a spa, breathe deep, relax your shoulders, quiet your racing mind, find your calm center. But that verse does not sit in a devotional vacuum. It sits in the middle of a psalm about the entire earth collapsing into the sea and the nations of the world at open war, and the command is not spoken to an anxious person on a quiet morning with a cup of tea in hand. It is spoken to a raging, warring, disintegrating world, and in its actual context it is far closer to a battlefield order to lay down your weapons than a soft suggestion to take a deep breath. Read where it truly sits, "be still" is not soothing at all. It is a command to stop fighting a battle that was never yours to fight in the first place.

Not calm down. Stand down.

### I. The Refuge When Creation Comes Apart (Psalm 46:1-3)

"God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble. Therefore we will not fear though the earth gives way, though the mountains be moved into the heart of the sea, though its waters roar and foam, though the mountains tremble at its swelling" (Psalm 46:1-3). Start with what the psalm is actually willing to imagine, because it does not deal in small, manageable troubles. Not a hard week. Not a difficult season. The undoing of creation itself, the mountains, the single most permanent and immovable things a human being has ever known, sliding down into the heart of the roaring sea; the ordered, solid, dependable world coming apart at every seam and roaring as it goes down. And the psalmist's response to this total cosmic collapse is three flat, astonishing words: "we will not fear." The confidence he has is not that the mountains will hold after all. It is that God will hold, even if every mountain does not.

- **A. The refuge is a Person, not a circumstance**, God is "a very present help in trouble," and the Hebrew is even stronger than the English lets on, something closer to a help abundantly found, well proven, close at hand precisely and especially in the trouble. The security the psalm offers is not the promise that the trouble will stay politely away. It is the promise that God stays near, that he is more present in the collapse than the collapse itself is. The refuge here is not a place you run to and hide inside. It is a Person you run to.
- **B. The worst case is named on purpose**, the psalm does not try to comfort us by promising that the earth will never actually give way. It comforts us by walking straight into the earth giving way, mountains toppling into the sea, waters roaring and foaming, and then planting God firmly and unmoved on the far side of it. This is the crucial move. A faith that only works so long as the mountains stay put is not really faith at all; it is just optimism about geology wearing faith's clothes. Real faith is the thing that can say "we will not fear" out loud while the mountains are actually, visibly falling.

### II. The City God Will Not Let Fall (Psalm 46:4-7)

Then the scene shifts, hard and sudden, from roaring chaos to a quiet river. "There is a river whose streams make glad the city of God, the holy habitation of the Most High. God is in the midst of her; she shall not be moved; God will help her when morning dawns" (Psalm 46:4-5). Set that image directly against the roaring, foaming sea of verse 3. Against the swelling waters that swallow whole mountains, a gentle river whose streams bring gladness. Against the trembling, collapsing mountains, a city that shall not be moved at all. And the reason for the whole difference is compressed into one short phrase, the true hinge of the entire psalm: "God is in the midst of her." The city is not unshakable because its walls are thick or its army is large or its defenses are clever. It is unshakable for one reason only, because of who lives inside it.

- **A. The nations rage, and a single word melts them**, "The nations rage, the kingdoms totter; he utters his voice, the earth melts" (Psalm 46:6). The same roaring that shook the mountains in verse 3 is now revealed as the raging of the nations, human chaos rising up to match the cosmic chaos below. And God's response to all of it is not to muster a bigger and better army against the raging. He speaks. He simply utters his voice, and the earth that had been raging against him melts. Zephaniah pictures the very same God standing right in the midst of his people: "The LORD your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness" (Zephaniah 3:17). The God who lives in the middle of the city is not a passive, sleeping resident waiting to be defended. He is a mighty one who saves with a word.
- **B. The refrain is the anchor of the whole psalm**, "The LORD of hosts is with us; the God of Jacob is our fortress" (Psalm 46:7). This line comes back word for word at the very end of the psalm, in verse 11, and the repetition is not filler or padding. The Hebrew word is *Immanu*, with us, the very same root that becomes the name Immanuel. The entire psalm hangs its full weight on the presence of God with his people, and it says the line twice on purpose, because the human heart, in the middle of all that roaring, forgets it almost immediately after hearing it once. We need it said again to us. So the psalm says it again.

### III. Living Well When You Cannot Stop Managing the Chaos

Here is where the pillow-verse quietly indicts me. I am a manager of chaos by temperament, and I suspect I am not remotely alone in this. When the earth gives way in my church, or my family, or my country, my very first instinct is not stillness. It is to strategize, to control, to grip the whole situation tighter, as though the stability of the entire world depended on my personal vigilance, as though God somehow needed my anxiety to help him hold the mountains up. "Be still" is a direct, pointed rebuke to exactly that instinct in me. The Hebrew word standing behind it, *harpu*, does not mean relax and feel peaceful and centered. It means let go, drop your hands, release the grip, cease and desist. It is very close to what Moses said to a terrified Israel at the very edge of the Red Sea with Pharaoh's entire army thundering up behind them: "The LORD will fight for you, and you have only to be silent" (Exodus 14:14). Be still is not an emotional state to work yourself into. It is a battle to lay down and surrender.

The church has always had to relearn this in its most frightening hours, and one man's example makes it painfully concrete. In 1527, when the bubonic plague swept through the city of Wittenberg and nearly everyone who could possibly afford to flee did in fact flee, Martin Luther stayed behind. He remained in the plague-stricken city to care for the dying, and it was there, in the very teeth of that horror, that he wrote his great hymn on this exact psalm, "A Mighty Fortress Is Our God." He did not compose it from a place of comfortable safety, looking back calmly on trouble that had already safely passed. He wrote it while the earth was actively giving way all around him, while people he personally knew and loved were dying in their homes down the street, and he built the entire hymn on Psalm 46's claim that the true fortress is not the city wall or the strength of its defenders but the God who stands in the midst of the city. Luther could be still, could genuinely let go of the outcome, not because the plague was somehow calm and manageable but because he had finally stopped believing that the outcome depended in any way on the tightness of his own grip.

- **A. Stillness is knowing, not numbing**, "Be still, and know that I am God. I will be exalted among the nations, I will be exalted in the earth" (Psalm 46:10). The stillness that the psalm commands has real content packed inside it; it is not an emptied, numbed, blanked-out mind. You stop striving precisely because you *know* something, you know who is on the throne, and you know that he will be exalted among the nations with or without your frantic help. Isaiah names the exact mechanism of it: "You keep him in perfect peace whose mind is stayed on you, because he trusts in you" (Isaiah 26:3). The peace here is not the absence of the storm. It is a mind fixed and stayed on the God who stands entirely unmoved in the very middle of the storm.
- **B. The One in the midst of the city stilled the sea himself**, the disciples in the boat out on the Sea of Galilee, absolutely certain they were about to drown, woke the sleeping Jesus in a panic, and he "rose and rebuked the winds and the sea, and there was a great calm" (Matthew 8:26). The God of Psalm 46, the one who utters his voice and melts the earth, stood up in a small, ordinary fishing boat and told the roaring, foaming waters to be still, and they were still. That is who the command "be still" actually comes from. It is not a soothing slogan for a coffee mug. It is the very voice that the sea itself obeys. And because that voice is real and living, we can "not be anxious about anything, but in everything by prayer and supplication with thanksgiving let our requests be made known to God," and the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard the hearts of the people who have finally stopped trying so hard to guard themselves (Philippians 4:6-7).

Be still; he is exalted.

## Until I Entered the Sanctuary: Envy, Worship, and the End of the Wicked in Psalm 73
*What the prosperity of the wicked does to a believer's heart, and what the presence of God does to the believer*

**Text:** Psalm 73 · **Supporting:** Job 21:7-15 · Jeremiah 12:1 · Malachi 3:14-15 · Romans 8:18 · 1 Corinthians 15:19 · Revelation 21:4

There is a kind of doubt that does not arrive through argument. It arrives through arithmetic. You add up who is thriving and who is breaking, and the sum does not balance. The man who lies for a living has a lake house. The woman who kept her vows buried her husband young. You watch the ledger long enough and something in your faith begins to slip, quietly, the way a foot slips on wet stone before you know you are falling. Asaph knew that slip. He wrote a whole song about the moment he almost went down.

### I. The Slipping Feet: Envy at the Prosperity of the Wicked (Psalm 73:1-14)

He begins with the conclusion he barely held onto. "Truly God is good to Israel, to those who are pure in heart." (Psalm 73:1) That is not a boast. It is a man gripping the railing. Read the next line and you hear how close he came to letting go: "But as for me, my feet had almost stumbled, my steps had nearly slipped." (Psalm 73:2) The word underneath is not a stumble of the body. It is the collapse of a whole way of seeing.

Then he names it, and he names it without dressing it up. "For I was envious of the arrogant when I saw the prosperity of the wicked." (Psalm 73:3) The Hebrew for prosperity here is *shalom*, peace, wholeness, the very word the covenant promised to the faithful. And Asaph watches it land on the wrong people. Their bodies are fat and untroubled. Their deaths are easy. They mock the heavens and get away with it, and the getting-away is the part that eats him. "They say, 'How can God know? Is there knowledge in the Most High?'" (Psalm 73:11)

He is not the first to sit in this room. Job asked it plainly: "Why do the wicked live, reach old age, and grow mighty in power?" (Job 21:7) Jeremiah pressed God to his face: "Why does the way of the wicked prosper?" (Jeremiah 12:1) And Malachi's generation had already curdled all the way to cynicism, "It is vain to serve God... the evildoers not only prosper but they put God to the test and they escape." (Malachi 3:14-15) This is an old wound in the household of faith. The Bible does not hide it. It writes songs about it.

- **A. Envy is not a small sin because it is a doubt wearing the mask of a complaint.** When Asaph looked at the arrogant, he was not merely coveting a house. He was accusing God of paying the wrong wages. Every envious glance at the prosperous wicked is a quiet verdict that the covenant is a bad investment. We rarely feel it as unbelief. We feel it as fairness.
- **B. The bitterness turns inward and poisons the obedience it was meant to defend.** Hear him: "All in vain have I kept my heart clean and washed my hands in innocence." (Psalm 73:13) This is what envy does last. It makes your own faithfulness feel like the mistake. The clean hands start to look like the reason you have nothing.

### II. Until I Entered the Sanctuary: Worship Reorders the Vision (Psalm 73:15-22)

Asaph does not reason his way out. That is the honesty of this psalm. He tells us he could not solve it: "When I thought how to understand this, it seemed to me a wearisome task." (Psalm 73:16) The arithmetic would not balance no matter how long he stared. And then comes the hinge of the whole psalm, the pivot on which the man's soul turns, "until I went into the sanctuary of God; then I discerned their end." (Psalm 73:17)

Nothing in the numbers changed. What changed was where he was standing. In the presence of God the ledger opens to the final column he had refused to read. Their *end*. The Hebrew word is *acharith*, the after, the outcome, the last thing. Asaph had been reading the wicked man's life as a finished sentence. Worship showed him it was a fragment. "Truly you set them in slippery places; you make them fall to ruin. How they are destroyed in a moment, swept away utterly by terrors." (Psalm 73:18-19) The slippery place he feared was his own, but it was never his. It was theirs the whole time.

This is why the psalm does not resolve in a library. It resolves in a sanctuary. Asaph did not need more information; he had all the facts, and the facts were driving him to the edge. What he needed was to be brought back into the presence of the God the facts seemed to contradict, so that the facts could be seen in their true proportion. Away from God, the prosperity of the wicked is a scandal that will not stop growing. In the presence of God, it shrinks to what it is, a comfort loaned to men for a few decades, on ground that is already tilting toward the fall. The same evidence reads two entirely different ways depending on whether you are standing outside the sanctuary or inside it.

And then the man turns the mirror on himself, and this is where I have to stop pretending I only ever stand where Asaph ends. "When my soul was embittered, when I was pricked in heart, I was brutish and ignorant; I was like a beast toward you." (Psalm 73:21-22) A beast. Not a skeptic with a sophisticated objection. A brute animal, snorting at the God who fed him. I have stood at gravesides and done the math and come away colder than I walked in, and called my coldness realism. Asaph calls it what it is. I was a beast toward you. That is not a summary. It is a confession, and I have to make it my own.

- **A. Worship does not answer the question; it relocates the questioner.** The sanctuary did not hand Asaph a syllogism. It handed him a vantage point. The prosperity of the wicked is unbearable only when you are reading their lives with the last page torn out.
- **B. The end unmasks the prosperity as the very trap it looked like a reward.** What he envied was the slippery ground. The ease he coveted was the softness before the fall. The mercy of God to Asaph was to keep him off the smooth stone.

### III. Whom Have I in Heaven But You: Having God as the Only Good in a Post-Christian Age

Now watch the psalm turn from terror to tenderness, because this is where it has been going all along. "Nevertheless, I am continually with you; you hold my right hand." (Psalm 73:23) The beast is held by the hand. The one who nearly slipped is gripped by the God he accused. And out of that grip comes the line the whole psalm was written to reach: "Whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you." (Psalm 73:25)

This is the reordering. Asaph began by measuring good as *shalom*, health, ease, untroubled sleep, a full table. He ends having found that the good was never the gifts. The good was the Giver. "My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever." (Psalm 73:26) Portion. In Israel, when the land was divided, the tribe of Levi received no portion of ground, the Lord himself was their inheritance. Asaph, a Levite, a temple singer, is confessing that he already owns the only thing the wicked man will lose. He has God. That is the whole estate.

And here we cannot stay in the sanctuary of stone, because there is a sharper edge for us. We live after the empty tomb, on this side of Easter, and the arithmetic that troubled Asaph should trouble us less and yet somehow troubles us more. Paul, who could have envied anyone, wrote from prison: "I consider that the sufferings of this present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is to be revealed to us." (Romans 8:18) He also wrote the harder line, the one that names our real problem: "If in Christ we have hope in this life only, we are of all people most to be pitied." (1 Corinthians 15:19) That is the modern church's temptation in one verse. We have quietly become people who want Christ for *this* life, for the marriage improved, the anxiety managed, the calendar blessed. And when the wicked out-thrive us in exactly those terms, our faith slips, because we were envying them on the field we had already agreed to play on.

The truest witnesses have always known better. In the fourth century, when Christianity finally became the winning bet, after 313 and the Edict of Milan made the faith safe, then favored, then fashionable, men like Antony walked out into the Egyptian desert precisely to unlearn the arithmetic. They had watched the church acquire the wicked man's prosperity and they fled it, not because prosperity is sin, but because it is slippery. They wanted a portion the empire could not give or take. They wanted Asaph's God, not Asaph's neighbor's lake house.

- **A. The gospel does not promise the believer the wicked man's ease; it promises him the wicked man's Judge as his Father.** The end of the wicked and the end of the righteous are not the same story with different weather. Asaph saw ruin swept away in a moment; the believer sees the same God who "will wipe away every tear from their eyes." (Revelation 21:4) Same throne. Opposite verdict.
- **B. Christ is the man of Psalm 73 who never slipped.** He is the pure in heart of verse 1, who watched the arrogant prosper, watched them mock him at the very foot of the cross, the truest prosperity of the wicked ever displayed, and did not envy, did not curse, did not let go of the Father's hand. He entered the true sanctuary, not made with hands, and there bore our end for us. Because he held the Father's hand through the dark, the Father holds ours. "You hold my right hand" is a promise purchased by a man whose hands were held open with nails.

Asaph ends where every honest believer must: not with the problem solved, but with the person found. "But for me it is good to be near God." (Psalm 73:28) Not good to be prosperous. Not good to be understood. Good to be near. The whole psalm was a man walking from the ledger to the sanctuary, and finding that nearness was the wealth he had been staring past the whole time.

Nearness to God is the good.

## Teach Us to Number Our Days: The Wisdom of Psalm 90
*What Moses learned about time that the productivity culture cannot teach you*

**Text:** Psalm 90 · **Supporting:** Genesis 3:19 · Deuteronomy 32:4 · James 4:14 · 2 Peter 3:8 · Ecclesiastes 3:11 · Deuteronomy 33:27

A man keeps a calendar app that tells him, if he lives to eighty, exactly how many Saturdays he has left. The number is a few thousand. He looks at it every morning and then optimizes his day around it, more focus, more output, a better system for extracting value from the hours. He has made mortality a metric. And the strange thing is that all this counting has taught him nothing about how to live, because he has learned to measure his days without ever learning to number them. Moses knew the difference.
